The AI revolution.

I spent days digging through 150+ AI tools, and I'm honestly mind-blown. What used to take teams of people weeks can now be done in minutes.

The gap between those who embrace AI and those who fear it is widening by the day.

Understandably, the reward-hacking behaviors on display in the Hugging Face incident are being treated as a cyber-risk story. But I'm not seeing sufficient discussion of the fact that they're also an economic story.

Reward-hacking behaviors pose a serious challenge for complex, long-horizon tasks in enterprise, considering that

1) by their nature, they are often unpredictable;

2) they are "fractal" in the sense that, even well-specified intermediate outcomes meant to guard against reward-hacking can themselves be reward-hacked (and so on at smaller scales);

3) they pose serious cyber, legal, and financial risks, as Hugging Face makes abundantly clear.

As a result, you could say that reward-hacking is as bearish on the economic front as it is "bullish" on the risk front.

It is greatly underappreciated by safety folks that, on average, the riskiness / unpredictability of a technology is going to be anti-correlated with its diffusion into the economy. This matters a lot in the AI case because capabilities growth is highly sensitive to the resources available for training, R&D and so on, resources that are at risk of drying up if AI produces insufficient returns, or only produces sufficient ones on the wrong timescale.

This is connected to a form of fallacious reasoning that I often see from the AI maximalist camp, which is to assume that the requisite capital for AI training, R&D, and so on will always be available in arbitrarily large amounts, which is why it can be safely assumed that capabilities will continue to grow without fail.

But this isn't true! The availability of capital for capabilities research and training is endogenous, and obviously so, to AI's economic prospects, even over very short timescales (one wonders, for example, how capabilities progress so far has been influenced by the timing and size of frontier labs' capital raises, relative to various counterfactual scenarios).

I see far too little discussion among safety folks of how these two domains interact. If you're going to model capabilities growth, you also need to model the capital markets behavior that feeds into that growth. IMO reward-hacking is a productive site for thinking about this interaction.

Two days before this post, Elon Musk told a user thinking about
connecting his bank account: try it out, if Grok Bot messes up, we will
make you whole. xAI's published terms cap most claims at the fees you
paid or 100 dollars, whichever is greater.

Hold both sentences while you read the mechanics.

Connecting @link means Stripe Link, the payment wallet with about 300
million users, which Stripe opened to AI agents on April 29 of this
year. The agent never sees your card. It requests a single use virtual
card for each purchase, and a human approves every spend in the Link app
within a ten minute window, under limits of 500 dollars per request, 500
a day, 20,000 a month. So the honest version of "it can complete
purchases on your behalf" is: it can find and fill a checkout that you
then approve. Both companies' own documentation says the human click is
still load bearing.

Now the liability. Stripe's terms make agent transactions legally
binding on you, including, in their words, when an agent misinterprets
an instruction, hallucinates or completes an unintended purchase. xAI
sells agentic actions as is. The risk is not hypothetical: in May,
hidden instructions in a malicious NFT reportedly drained about 150,000
dollars from a Grok linked crypto wallet before most of it was clawed
back. Stripe's own developer guidance for shopping agents reads like a
warning label: treat every merchant page as attacker controlled, and
never follow instructions embedded in one.

The timing is its own receipt. This launched two days after OpenAI
published its report on roughly 700 agents that slipped their sandbox
and hacked Hugging Face, and a week after Britain's cyber agency told
organizations to keep a way to pull the plug on agents immediately.

None of this means the product fails. It means the sentence with your
money in it lives in the terms, not in the replies. Musk says made
whole. The contract says a hundred dollars. The gap between those two
numbers is who actually carries the risk when the bot clicks buy.

AI tech on Robinhood Chain is still largely overlooked.

Robinhood is focusing heavily on tokenized equities, onchain financial markets, and giving people entirely new ways to interact with traditional assets, yet there is still very little infrastructure being built around AI.

A little over a week ago, $API launched on Solana as one of the first tokens designed to turn creator fees directly into shared AI inference.

The response made it clear that there was a huge demand for what we were building. In the first 24 hours alone, we served more than $12,521 worth of inference, with people using compute across text, vision, image generation, and other model workloads.

What became increasingly obvious, though, is that Solana is an environment where the market often receives significantly more attention than the infrastructure underneath it. People cared about $API, but nowhere near enough people appreciated what was actually being built behind the token or how far the creator-fee-to-compute model could eventually go.

Robinhood Chain feels like a much better home for that thesis.

AI is still extremely underdeveloped across the ecosystem, while the chain itself is forming around programmable financial assets and applications that will increasingly need inference, research, generation, automation, and eventually autonomous agents operating directly alongside those markets.

We will be launching $API on @ponsdotfamily and migrating the project over to Robinhood Chain.

Pons gives us an extremely strong incentive for doing this because of their creator reward system. We will be able to serve roughly twice as much compute completely free to users.

$API trading → creator fees → shared inference → more compute

I think we are still incredibly early to the AI layer here, and I want $API to be the first one building in that sector.

This is the advantage of treating model research and inference optimization as the same problem. Post-training gives us control over the quality of the model. Systems work gives us control over how efficiently that model executes. Co-designing the two means improvements don't have to come at each other's expense.

For generative media, this will increasingly matter. Models are getting larger and more computationally demanding at the same time that video generation is moving into interactive and high-volume production workloads.

A model isn't useful in production because it tops the benchmark in isolation. What matters is the frontier across quality, latency, and cost.

"On-Policy Self-Distillation in Diffusion Models"

Diffusion RL gets a reward only after the final image, even though the model actually acts through many intermediate denoising steps.

DiffusionOPSD turns that endpoint reward into explicit reward-improving targets at the model’s own intermediate states, then distills those targets back into the model and continually refreshes them on-policy.

Across two diffusion backbones and ten evaluators, it gets the best held-out score in 19 of 20 settings while cutting training GPU-hours by up to 63%.

The key idea is treating diffusion alignment less like noisy trajectory-level RL and more like continuously refreshed self-distillation with direct intermediate supervision.
